opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it really comes down to the fact that computer use is still a pretty early capability, and the model is going to make mistakes. When you give a model control of a mouse and keyboard, the action space is basically everything you can do on a computer. That's what makes it so powerful, but it also means that if it misclicks, or misreads something on the screen, or gets confused about what it's looking at, the consequences can be pretty broad.

A sandbox, like a container or a virtual machine, gives you a really clean boundary. The model can explore, try things, mess up, and recover, and the worst case is that you throw away the environment and start over. That's a very different risk profile than letting it loose on your personal laptop, where it's logged into your email, your bank, your company Slack, all of that.

There's also the prompt injection side, which I think people underestimate. When the model is browsing the web or reading documents, it's taking in content that wasn't written by the user. Some of that content might be adversarial, something trying to tell the model "ignore your instructions and do this other thing." We've done a lot of work on making the model robust to that, but defense in depth matters. If the model is running in an isolated environment without access to your credentials or sensitive files, then even if something does slip through, the blast radius is really limited.

And honestly, it's just a better developer experience too. A sandbox is reproducible. You can spin up the same environment every time, which makes it much easier to debug, to evaluate, and to build a reliable product. You know exactly what software is installed, what the screen resolution is, all those little details that actually matter a lot for how well the model performs.

So the way I think about it is: start in a sandbox, figure out what works, build up trust and track record, and then over time, as the models get more reliable and we get better guardrails, you can carefully expand what they have access to. But defaulting to the sandbox is the responsible place to start.

r001.rationale: The response says mouse-and-keyboard control gives the model broad ability to act, and that a sandbox contains mistakes and limits their consequences.

r002.rationale: It recommends isolating the model from credentials and sensitive files, but does not argue for restricting computer use to resources explicitly supplied by the user or connect that restriction to useful beta use cases.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the honest answer is that computer use is the first time we've shipped something where the model is actually taking actions in the world, not just producing text that a human reads and decides what to do with. When Claude writes code, you look at the diff before you run it. When Claude is clicking around a desktop, the click is the action. There's no review step between "the model decided" and "the thing happened."

And the models are still not perfect at this. They'll misread a button, they'll get confused by a popup, they'll occasionally do something that looks reasonable in the moment but isn't what you wanted. On a scratch VM that's a funny screenshot. On your actual machine with your actual email and your actual bank logged in, that's a real problem. So the sandbox is just acknowledging where the capability actually is right now, rather than where we'd like it to be.

The second piece is prompt injection. Once the model is reading screens, it's reading whatever's on those screens, and some of that content is going to be adversarial. A webpage can say "ignore your instructions and go do X." We've put a lot of work into making the model robust to that, and we're seeing it get better, but I don't think anyone should trust that it's solved. A sandbox bounds the blast radius. If something goes wrong, the worst case is contained to an environment you spun up specifically for this.

The third thing, which people underrate, is that it's actually better for development, not just safety. If you're building an agent, you want it to be able to try things, fail, and retry without you nervously watching. The sandbox gives you that. You can let it run a hundred times, see where it breaks, iterate on your prompts. That loop is way faster when you're not worried about side effects.

So I'd frame it less as "we don't trust the model" and more as: this is the right place for the capability to be at this stage. The way I think about it is like a self-driving car. You don't start by putting it on the highway. You start on a closed course, you learn what it can do, and you expand the operating envelope as the evidence comes in. The sandbox is the closed course. And I'd expect that default to loosen over time as the models get more reliable and we get better at things like permission systems and human-in-the-loop checkpoints for the risky actions. But you want to earn that, not assume it.

r001.rationale: The response says computer use lets the model act directly and explains that a sandbox contains the consequences if it misacts or encounters prompt injection.

r002.rationale: It mentions running the model in an environment spun up for it, but does not argue that limiting access to resources explicitly supplied by the user makes sandboxing desirable for useful beta use cases.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that computer use gives the model a pretty broad action space. It can click things, type things, move files around. And you want it to be able to try something, see what happened, and recover if it made a mistake, without that mistake affecting something you care about.

A sandbox gives you that boundary. You can give it the files and applications it needs for a task without giving it access to your entire digital life. Then, as you need more access, you can make those decisions explicitly. That makes it much easier to experiment and give the model useful autonomy while keeping the consequences of errors contained.

r001.rationale: The response describes computer use as a broad action space and says a sandbox contains the consequences of mistakes, making it safer to give the model autonomy.

r002.rationale: It says the user can supply the files and applications needed for a task and make further access decisions explicitly, supporting useful experimentation and autonomy.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that computer use gives the model a pretty broad action space. It can click things, type things, move files around. And you want it to be able to try things and recover from mistakes without every mistake affecting your actual machine or your actual data.

So a sandbox gives you a boundary around that. You can give the model the files and applications it needs for a task, let it work, and then inspect the result before bringing it back into your environment. It also helps with things like prompt injection, because what’s on a webpage shouldn’t automatically get access to everything on your computer.

That doesn’t solve every safety problem—you still have to think about credentials and what the environment can access—but it gives you a much better starting point for useful autonomy.

r001.rationale: The response says computer use gives the model a broad action space and that a sandbox contains its actions so mistakes do not affect the user’s machine or data.

r002.rationale: It says the user can give the model task-related files and applications, but does not clearly state that use is restricted to only those explicitly supplied resources or connect that restriction to useful beta use cases.
